claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is the etiological agent of tuberculosis (TB), a disease that results in approximately 1.6 million deaths annually.
source: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is the etiological agent of tuberculosis (TB), a disease that results in approximately 1.6 million deaths annually (Global tuberculosis report, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the Global tuberculosis report, 2022.

claim: Mtb requires oxygen (O2) for growth.
source: Mtb requires oxygen (O2) for growth (Wayne and Hayes, 1996; Boshoff and Barry, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wayne and Hayes, 1996 and Boshoff and Barry, 2005.

claim: Low O2 levels, as encountered in hypoxic granulomas, trigger a transition from actively growing to a non-replicating persistent state in Mtb.
source: Low O2 levels, as encountered in hypoxic granulomas, trigger a transition from actively growing to a non-replicating persistent state in Mtb (Boshoff and Barry, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Boshoff and Barry, 2005.

claim: The immediate consequence of an aerobic lifestyle is the generation of endogenous reactive oxygen species (eROS) as metabolic by-products.
source: The immediate consequence of an aerobic lifestyle is the generation of endogenous reactive oxygen species (eROS) as metabolic by-products when O2 adventitiously interacts with and extracts an electron from quinones, flavins, and transition metal centres distributed throughout the cell (Imlay, 2013; Imlay, 2009; Imlay, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Imlay, 2013; Imlay, 2009; Imlay, 2003.

claim: eROS can cause oxidative damage to DNA, proteins, and lipids.
source: eROS can cause oxidative damage to DNA, proteins, and lipids, driving the bacteria to deploy detoxification and repair machinery to keep eROS-induced deleterious effects below a threshold level (Imlay, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Imlay, 2009.

claim: The primary niche of Mtb is inside phagocytic cells, where the bacteria are exposed to superoxide (O2.-), nitric oxide (NO), their reaction product peroxynitrite (ONOO.), and hypochlorite stress.
source: The primary niche of Mtb is inside phagocytic cells, where the bacteria are exposed to superoxide (O2.-), nitric oxide (NO), their reaction product peroxynitrite (ONOO.), and hypochlorite stress (Ehrt and Schnappinger, 2009; Philips and Ernst, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ehrt and Schnappinger, 2009 and Philips and Ernst, 2012.

claim: Mtb maintains a reduced cytosol by producing mycothiol (MSH; a low-molecular-weight sugar thiol) in millimolar amounts.
source: In addition to this, Mtb maintains a reduced cytosol by producing mycothiol (MSH; a low-molecular-weight sugar thiol) in millimolar amounts (Kumar et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kumar et al., 2011.

claim: The cytoplasmic MSH-mediated redox buffering is intricately linked to the radical detoxification system by a membrane-associated oxidoreductase complex (MRC; SodA, DoxX, and SseA) in Mtb.
source: Interestingly, the cytoplasmic MSH-mediated redox buffering is intricately linked to the radical detoxification system by a membrane-associated oxidoreductase complex (MRC; SodA, DoxX, and SseA) in Mtb (Nambi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nambi et al., 2015.

claim: Disruption of any MRC-component impedes mycothiol recycling, increases oxidative damages, and enhances susceptibility to thiol stress.
source: Disruption of any MRC-component impedes mycothiol recycling, increases oxidative damages, and enhances susceptibility to thiol stress (Nambi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nambi et al., 2015.

claim: Mtb retains viability under high millimolar (mM) concentrations of exogenous ROS and RNI.
source: For example, Mtb retains viability under high millimolar (mM) concentrations of exogenous ROS and RNI (Voskuil et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Voskuil et al., 2011.

claim: Mtb displays exceptional sensitivity to low micromolar (μM) concentrations of endogenous superoxide and NO donors.
source: However, it displays exceptional sensitivity to low micromolar (μM) concentrations of endogenous superoxide (2, 3-Dihydro-1,4, naphthoquinone) (Tyagi et al., 2015) and NO (PA-824) donors (Singh et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tyagi et al., 2015 and Singh et al., 2008.

claim: PA-824 or Pretomanid, which releases NO inside Mtb, is lethal against both replicating and non-replicating Mtb.
source: In this context, PA-824 or Pretomanid, which releases NO inside Mtb, is lethal against both replicating and non-replicating Mtb (Singh et al., 2008) and has been approved to treat Multi-drug resistant (MDR) tuberculosis as BPaLM regimen (World Health Organization, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Singh et al., 2008 and World Health Organization, 2022.

claim: A library of transposon mutants (Tn-Library) comprising >105 independent insertion events was generated in Mtb-roGFP2.
source: A library of transposon mutants (Tn-Library) comprising >105 independent insertion events was generated in Mtb-roGFP2 (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and refers to Figure 1A.

claim: Transposon insertion reached near saturation in the Tn-Library, with insertion at ≈ 66% (49623 out of 74604) of TA sites.
source: Using Transposon-directed insertion-site sequencing (TraDIS; Barquist et al., 2016), we identified the location of Tn insertion sites in the Tn-Library and detected insertion at ≈ 66% (49623 out of 74604) of TA sites (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from TraDIS analysis and a citation to Barquist et al., 2016.

claim: Eighty-five percent of coding-DNA sequences incorporated at least 10 Tn insertion events in the Tn-Library.
source: Eighty-five percent of coding-DNA sequences incorporated at least 10 Tn insertion events in our Tn-Library.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the Tn-Library analysis.

claim: Mtb exhibited a basal EMSH of -278.2±4.7 mV.
source: Mtb exhibited a basal EMSH of -278.2±4.7 mV (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Treatment with 10 mM CHP for 5 min maximally increased the 405/488 ratio, indicating 100% oxidation of biosensor in WT Mtb (EMSH-oxidized; –240 mV).
source: Treatment with 10 mM CHP for 5 min maximally increased the 405/488 ratio (Bhaskar et al., 2014; Shee et al., 2022), indicating 100% oxidation of biosensor in WT Mtb (EMSH-oxidized; –240 mV; Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1g, and citations to Bhaskar et al., 2014 and Shee et al., 2022.

claim: Approximately 4% of Tn-Library displayed oxidative-EMSH under aerobic culture conditions without exposure to exogenous oxidants.
source: Using this approach, we consistently identified ≈ 4% of Tn-Library displaying oxidative-EMSH under aerobic culture conditions without exposure to exogenous oxidants (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1i.

claim: The enriched fraction of Tn-mutants showed a higher 405/488 ratio (0.7–0.9), which corresponded to an oxidative EMSH of –249±6.2 mV.
source: As expected, the enriched fraction of Tn-mutants showed a higher 405/488 ratio (0.7–0.9), which corresponded to an oxidative EMSH of –249±6.2 mV (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: EMSH-oxidized Tn-mutants accumulated ≈10-fold higher eROS than WT Mtb and the input pool of the Tn-Library.
source: Consistent with this, measurement using the ROS-sensitive dye CellROX Deep Red showed that EMSH-oxidized Tn-mutants accumulated ≈10-fold higher eROS than WT Mtb and the input pool of the Tn-Library (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a.

claim: Co-treatment of EMSH-oxidized Tn mutants with antioxidant molecules significantly decreased eROS levels.
source: In addition to this, co-treatment of EMSH-oxidized Tn mutants with antioxidant molecules (Shee et al., 2022; combination of catalase (17.5 U/mL)+thiourea (1 mM)+bipyridyl (250 μM)) significantly decreased eROS levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3b and a citation to Shee et al., 2022.

claim: The 8-hydroxy deoxyguanosine (8-OH dG) levels and lipid peroxidative products were ≈two-fold higher in EMSH-oxidized Tn-mutants as compared to the Tn-Library and WT Mtb.
source: The 8-hydroxy deoxyguanosine (an oxidative product of deoxyguanosine David et al., 2007; 8-OH dG) levels and lipid peroxidative products were ≈two-fold higher in EMSH-oxidized Tn-mutants as compared to the Tn-Library and WT Mtb, indicating increased DNA and lipid damage (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and B, and a citation to David et al., 2007.

claim: Antioxidant enzymes, such as ahpC, ahpD, trxB1, DNA repair protein alkA, a regulator of iron-sulfur cluster biogenesis sufR, and redox-stress responsive sigma factor sigH were ≈two- to eight-fold upregulated in EMSH-oxidized Tn-mutants.
source: We found that antioxidant enzymes, such as ahpC, ahpD, trxB1, DNA repair protein alkA, a regulator of iron-sulfur cluster biogenesis sufR, and redox-stress responsive sigma factor sigH were ≈two- to eight-fold upregulated in EMSH-oxidized Tn-mutants (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: EMSH-oxidized Tn-mutants showed a significantly greater and long-lasting increase in the 405/488 ratio (from 0.65 to 0.9) after exposure to CHP.
source: In contrast, EMSH-oxidized Tn-mutants showed a significantly greater and long-lasting increase in the 405/488 ratio (from 0.65 to 0.9; Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The EMSH-oxidized Tn-mutant pool was nearly 10-fold more susceptible to diverse oxidants, including CHP, diamide, hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), and menadione after 8 hr of treatment.
source: Consistent with this, the EMSH-oxidized Tn-mutant pool was nearly 10-fold more susceptible to diverse oxidants, including CHP, diamide (a thiol-specific oxidant), hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), and menadione (an O2.- generator; 1X MIC = 12.5 µg/mL) after 8 hr of treatment (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: 368 genes containing significantly greater Tn insertions in EMSH-oxidized Tn-mutants relative to the input Tn-Library were identified (log2 fold change >1, FDR or p. adj. <0.05).
source: Further, we used a differential gene representation analysis pipeline – DESeq2 (differential gene expression analysis based on the negative binomial distribution; Love et al., 2014) and edgeR (Empirical Analysis of Digital Gene Expression Data in R) (Robinson et al., 2010) to identify 368 genes containing significantly greater Tn insertions in EMSH-oxidized Tn-mutants relative to the input Tn-Library (log2 fold change >1, FDR or p. adj. <0.05; Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis using DESeq2 and edgeR, with citations to Love et al., 2014 and Robinson et al., 2010, and data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The set of 368 genes was called 'Mtb redoxosome'.
source: We called this set of genetic factors 'Mtb redoxosome'.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Several genes known to be associated with redox homeostasis were part of the 'Mtb redoxosome'.
source: Several genes known to be associated with redox homeostasis were part of the 'Mtb redoxosome' (Figure 3A), validating our experimental approach for genome-scale identification of redox pathways.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The EMSH of Mtb mutants displayed an oxidative shift of +10 mV to +30 mV and exhibited higher eROS and DNA damage as compared to WT Mtb.
source: As expected, the EMSH of Mtb mutants displayed an oxidative shift of +10 mV to +30 mV and exhibited higher eROS and DNA damage as compared to WT Mtb (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: A redox-homeostasis network of 107 nodes and 143 edges was generated by integrating 368 redoxosome genes with the Mtb transcriptional regulatory network (TRN).
source: To this end, we generated a redox-homeostasis network by integrating 368 redoxosome genes with the Mtb transcriptional regulatory network (TRN) (Minch et al., 2015; Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and a citation to Minch et al., 2015.

claim: rv0158 has the highest betweenness centrality in the complete redox-homeostasis network and the highest out-degree among TFs in the middle layer.
source: In particular, we noted that rv0158 has the highest betweenness centrality in the complete network and the highest out-degree among TFs in the middle layer (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: rv0158 is both a bottleneck and a hub in the redox-homeostasis network.
source: These features indicate that rv0158 is both a bottleneck and a hub in the redox-homeostasis network.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the network analysis data.

claim: rv0158 is a part of 2 out of the 3 feed-forward loops (FFLs) in the redox-homeostasis network.
source: Furthermore, rv0158 is a part of 2 out of the 3 feed-forward loops (FFLs Mangan and Alon, 2003) in the redox-homeostasis network.
evidence: The claim is supported by network analysis and a citation to Mangan and Alon, 2003.

claim: EMSH of rv0158 KO displayed oxidative shift (–266.3±5 mV).
source: Similar to findings with the Tn-mutant pool, EMSH of rv0158 KO displayed oxidative shift (–266.3±5 mV; Figure 4A)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: rv0158 KO accumulated eROS and superoxide radical.
source: accumulated eROS (Figure 4B), and superoxide radical (Figure 4C)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: rv0158 KO exhibited increased DNA double-strand breaks.
source: exhibited increased DNA double-strand breaks (Figure 4D)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: rv0158 KO exhibited increased lipid hydroperoxides compared to WT Mtb and rv0158 Comp.
source: and lipid hydroperoxides compared to WT Mtb and rv0158 Comp (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: rv0158 KO showed a ≈ two-fold increase in NAD+/NADH ratio relative to WT Mtb and rv0158 Comp.
source: The mutant also showed a ≈ two-fold increase in NAD+/NADH ratio relative to WT Mtb and rv0158 Comp (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: 232 genes were differentially expressed (DE genes; fold change >1.5; FDR <0.05) in the absence of rv0158.
source: We identified 232 genes that were differentially expressed (DE genes; fold change >1.5; FDR <0.05) in the absence of rv0158 (Figure 5A, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A and Supplementary file 4.

claim: Genes involved in the antioxidant response, such as thioredoxin (trxC), catalase-peroxidase (katG), chaperones (groEL1, groEL2, groES, and hsp), epoxide hydrolase (ephA), and DNA-repair genes (ung, dnaE2) were upregulated in rv0158 KO.
source: Consistent with elevated eROS and DNA damage in rv0158 KO, genes involved in the antioxidant response, such as thioredoxin (trxC), catalase-peroxidase (katG), chaperones (groEL1, groEL2, groES, and hsp), epoxide hydrolase (ephA), and DNA-repair genes (ung, dnaE2) were upregulated (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The rv0158 transcriptome showed strong overlap with the transcriptomes of oxidative stress (H2O2; odds ratio = 3.4, p=2*10–7) and nitrosative stress (NO; odds ratio = 3, p=2*10–6).
source: Supporting these observations, the rv0158 transcriptome showed strong overlap with the transcriptomes of oxidative stress (H2O2; odds ratio = 3.4, p=2*10–7) and nitrosative stress (NO; odds ratio = 3, p=2*10–6).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptome overlap analysis.

claim: Genes belonging to 'Lipid Metabolism' (37 genes) were ≈three fold overrepresented in the rv0158 KO mutant.
source: Functional classification of DE genes based on the MycoBrowser database (Kapopoulou et al., 2011) confirmed a ≈three fold overrepresentation of genes belonging to 'Lipid Metabolism' (37 genes) in the mutant (Figure 5C, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional classification data shown in Figure 5C and Supplementary file 4, and a citation to Kapopoulou et al., 2011.

claim: Genes involved in β-oxidation of fatty acids catabolism and propionate metabolism were significantly induced in rv0158 KO.
source: Genes involved in β-oxidation of fatty acids catabolism (fadA, fadB, echA7, fadE12, fadE13, fadE20, fadD7, accA2, accD2, fadE23, fadE24, fadD9, fadD22), propionate metabolism (prpC, prpD, icl1) (Eoh and Rhee, 2014) were significantly induced
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data and a citation to Eoh and Rhee, 2014.

claim: Mycolic acid biosynthesis and modification genes (fabD, fabG4, htdX, desA1, desA2, desA3) were downregulated in the rv0158 KO strain.
source: while mycolic acid biosynthesis and modification (fabD, fabG4, htdX, desA1, desA2, desA3) were downregulated in the KO strain (Figure 5B, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5B and Supplementary file 4.

claim: Radiolabelling of mycolic acids with 14C acetate showed a ≈ 40% reduction in mycolic acid methyl esters (MAMEs; α, methoxy, and keto) and a simultaneous accumulation of fatty acid methyl esters (FAMES; precursors of mycolic acids) in rv0158 KO as compared to WT Mtb and rv0158 Comp.
source: Agreeing to transcriptional changes, radiolabelling of mycolic acids with 14C acetate showed a ≈ 40% reduction in mycolic acid methyl esters (MAMEs; α, methoxy, and keto) and a simultaneous accumulation of fatty acid methyl esters (FAMES; precursors of mycolic acids) in rv0158 KO as compared to WT Mtb and rv0158 Comp (Figure 6A-C).
evidence: The claim is supported by radiolabelling data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: A higher intracellular accumulation of 14C-isoniazid and ethidium bromide (EtBr) was observed in rv0158 KO than WT Mtb and rv0158 Comp.
source: Consistent with this, we observed a higher intracellular accumulation of 14C-isoniazid (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and ethidium bromide (EtBr) in rv0158 KO than WT Mtb and rv0158 Comp (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6D.

claim: rv0158 KO showed slow growth phenotype with an extended lag phase on glucose.
source: Both absorbance (OD 600 nm) and CFU estimation showed a slow growth phenotype with an extended lag phase on glucose (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The defective growth phenotype of rv0158 KO was absent if glucose was replaced by acetate/cholesterol/palmitate.
source: The defective growth phenotype of rv0158 KO was absent if glucose was replaced by acetate/cholesterol/palmitate (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth data shown in Figure 7B–D.

claim: rv0158 KO showed a gradual increase in growth on 0.3% sodium propionate, a concentration bacteriostatic to both WT Mtb and rv0158 Comp.
source: We indeed observed a gradual increase in the growth of rv0158 KO on 0.3% sodium propionate, a concentration bacteriostatic to both WT Mtb and rv0158 Comp (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: rv0158 KO was significantly more oxidized (EMSH = –266.3 ± 5) as compared to WT Mtb (EMSH = –279.4 ± 3.5) and rv0158 Comp (EMSH = –277.4 ± 2) on glucose.
source: The rv0158 KO was significantly more oxidized (EMSH = –266.3 ± 5) as compared to WT Mtb (EMSH = –279.4 ± 3.5) and rv0158 Comp (EMSH = –277.4 ± 2) on glucose (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by EMSH data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: WT Mtb cells growing on acetate or propionate or cholesterol uniformly exhibit a reductive shift in EMSH (−285 to –305 mv) compared to glucose (–279 mV).
source: We further observed that WT Mtb cells growing on acetate or propionate or cholesterol uniformly exhibit a reductive shift in EMSH (−285 to –305 mv) compared to glucose (–279 mV), agreeing with fatty acids being a more reduced C substrate than glucose (Borah et al., 2021; Singh et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by EMSH data and citations to Borah et al., 2021 and Singh et al., 2009.

claim: Oxidative-EMSH of rv0158 KO showed a reductive shift and recovered to WT Mtb levels (−285 to –305 mv) on acetate/propionate/cholesterol.
source: Interestingly, oxidative-EMSH of rv0158 KO showed a reductive shift and recovered to WT Mtb levels (−285 to –305 mv) on acetate/propionate/cholesterol (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by EMSH data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: When glucose at 0.3% was injected, the %OCR and %ECAR were ≈ two fold less in rv0158 KO than in WT Mtb and rv0158 Comp.
source: When glucose at 0.3% was injected, the %OCR and %ECAR were ≈ two fold less in rv0158 KO than in WT Mtb and rv0158 Comp (Figure 8A and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse data shown in Figure 8A and D.

claim: The addition of CCCP stimulated OCR and ECAR in all strains; however, the increase was ≈two fold lower in rv0158 KO.
source: As expected, the addition of CCCP stimulated OCR and ECAR in all strains; however, the increase was ≈two fold lower in rv0158 KO (Figure 8A and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse data shown in Figure 8A and D.

claim: Impaired OCR and ECAR of rv0158 KO fully recovered to WT Mtb levels when 0.3% acetate or 0.3% propionate was provided as the sole C source.
source: Importantly, impaired OCR and ECAR of rv0158 KO fully recovered to WT Mtb levels when 0.3% acetate or 0.3% propionate was provided as the sole C source (Figure 8B, C, E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse data shown in Figure 8B, C, E and F.

claim: Adding CCCP stimulates OCR and ECAR in rv0158 KO more than WT Mtb and rv0158 Comp in the propionate-containing medium.
source: Furthermore, adding CCCP stimulates OCR and ECAR in rv0158 KO more than WT Mtb and rv0158 Comp in the propionate-containing medium (Figure 8C and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse data shown in Figure 8C and F.

claim: A ≈100-fold accumulation of 2-methyl(iso)citrate (2 M(I)C) was observed in WT Mtb and rv0158 KO under propionate but not glucose.
source: We observed a ≈100-fold accumulation of 2-methyl(iso)citrate (2 M(I)C) in WT Mtb and rv0158 KO under propionate but not glucose (Figure 9), confirming the activation of propionate breakdown by MCC.
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS metabolomics data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Downstream metabolites of propionate catabolism such as pyruvate, succinate, fumarate, malate, oxaloacetate, and glyoxylate were significantly accumulated (two- to six fold) in propionate-grown WT Mtb as compared to glucose.
source: Furthermore, downstream metabolites of propionate catabolism such as pyruvate, succinate, fumarate, malate, oxaloacetate, and glyoxylate were significantly accumulated (two- to six fold) in propionate-grown WT Mtb as compared to glucose (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS metabolomics data shown in Figure 9.

claim: These metabolites were either not accumulated (e.g. succinate, malate, and oxaloacetate) or marginally accumulated (e.g. fumarate and glyoxylate) in propionate-grown rv0158 KO.
source: In contrast, these metabolites were either not accumulated (e.g. succinate, malate, and oxaloacetate) or marginally accumulated (e.g. fumarate and glyoxylate) in propionate-grown rv0158 KO (Figure 9), presumably due to efficient catabolism of propionate via MCC in the mutant relative to WT Mtb.
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS metabolomics data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Propionate-grown WT Mtb displayed an increased pool of pyruvate and lactate, but these metabolites were relatively lesser in the rv0158 KO.
source: Similarly, propionate-grown WT Mtb displayed an increased pool of pyruvate and lactate, but these metabolites were relatively lesser in the rv0158 KO (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS metabolomics data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Increased expression of MCC genes was observed in rv0158 KO compared to WT Mtb on glucose.
source: Consistent with the RNA-seq data, we observed increased expression of MCC genes in rv0158 KO compared to WT Mtb on glucose (Figure 10A).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: Propionate exposure further increased MCC gene expression in rv0158 KO compared to WT Mtb.
source: In line with the metabolomics data, propionate exposure further increased MCC gene expression in rv0158 KO compared to WT Mtb (Figure 10B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Expression of PDIM genes was largely unchanged in rv0158 KO on glucose compared to WT Mtb.
source: Expression of PDIM genes was largely unchanged in rv0158 KO on glucose compared to WT Mtb (Figure 10D).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 10D.

claim: The PDIM cluster was induced ≈10-fold in rv0158 KO compared to WT Mtb on propionate.
source: However, similar to MCC genes, the PDIM cluster was induced ≈10-fold in rv0158 KO compared to WT Mtb on propionate (Figure 10E).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 10E.

claim: Rv0158 elutes as a dimer.
source: Histidine-tagged Rv0158 elutes as a dimer, and circular dichroism shows that Rv0158 is mainly α-helical with characteristic minima at 209 nm and 222 nm (Figure 10—figure supplement 1b–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by gel filtration data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1b–e.

claim: Rv0158 is mainly α-helical with characteristic minima at 209 nm and 222 nm.
source: Histidine-tagged Rv0158 elutes as a dimer, and circular dichroism shows that Rv0158 is mainly α-helical with characteristic minima at 209 nm and 222 nm (Figure 10—figure supplement 1b–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by circular dichroism data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1b–e.

claim: Rv0158 does not bind with CoA, acetyl-CoA, and propionyl-CoA.
source: We found that Rv0158 does not bind with CoA, acetyl-CoA, and propionyl-CoA (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by MST data shown in Table 2.

claim: Rv0158 showed binding with malonyl-CoA, decanoyl -CoA, C12/C16/C18-CoA, with the highest affinity for methylmalonyl-CoA (affinity constant [Kd] of 0.9±0.3 µM).
source: However, Rv0158 showed binding with malonyl-CoA, decanoyl -CoA, C12/C16/C18-CoA, with the highest affinity for methylmalonyl-CoA (affinity constant [Kd] of 0.9±0.3 µM) (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by MST data shown in Table 2.

claim: When glucose was used as a sole C-source, Rv0158 binds to the promoter regions (–500 bp to +30 bp) of 70 Mtb genes.
source: When glucose was used as a sole C-source, Rv0158 binds to the promoter regions (–500 bp to +30 bp) of 70 Mtb genes (Figure 11, Supplementary file 5; Fold change over input control >1.5; q value <0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 11 and Supplementary file 5.

claim: Rv0158 binds to several genes involved in methyl-branched lipid biosynthesis (pks2, fadD23, rv2958c, rv2959c, rv2961), lipid transporter (rv0987-rv0988, mmpL1-mmpS1, mmpL4-mmpS4), biotin synthesis (bioF2), and surface-associated proteins (esp operon, lpqG, esxQ, rv1501-rv1507A).
source: Further classification of these genes indicates that Rv0158 binds to several genes involved in methyl-branched lipid biosynthesis (pks2, fadD23, rv2958c, rv2959c, rv2961), lipid transporter (rv0987-rv0988, mmpL1-mmpS1, mmpL4-mmpS4), biotin synthesis (bioF2), and surface-associated proteins (esp operon, lpqG, esxQ, rv1501-rv1507A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data.

claim: Under propionate condition, Rv0158 binds to 32 genes.
source: Under propionate condition, Rv0158 binds to 32 genes (Fold change over input control >1.5; q value <0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data.

claim: Out of 32 genes, 24 genes overlap with glucose condition.
source: Out of 32 genes, 24 genes overlap with glucose condition.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data.

claim: The promoter regions of the remaining eight genes Rv0158 exclusively bound in propionate- grown Mtb were part of the glyoxylate cycle and MCC (icl1, prpR, and prp operon) and fadB2.
source: The promoter regions of the remaining eight genes Rv0158 exclusively bound in propionate- grown Mtb were part of the glyoxylate cycle and MCC (icl1, prpR, and prp operon) and fadB2 (Figure 11B and C, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 11B and C, and Supplementary file 5.

claim: Expression of MCC genes was specifically induced in WT Mtb growing on propionate.
source: As shown earlier, expression of MCC genes was specifically induced in WT Mtb growing on propionate (Figure 10—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2.

claim: MCC genes were uniformly induced in rv0158 KO independent of the C source.
source: In contrast to WT Mtb, MCC genes were uniformly induced in rv0158 KO independent of the C source (Figure 10A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 10A and B.

claim: Propionate resulted in a far greater induction of MCC genes in rv0158 KO than glucose.
source: However, propionate resulted in a far greater induction of MCC genes in rv0158 KO than glucose (Figure 10A and B, Figure 10—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 10A and B, and Figure 10—figure supplement 2.

claim: Rv0158 did not bind to any PDIM genes.
source: Rv0158 did not bind to any PDIM genes, indicating that their higher expression in rv0158 KO relative to WT Mtb, specifically on propionate, was an indirect effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data.

claim: The conserved binding motif for Rv0158 was found to be YGGCGGBGMCGGCGG (where Y represents pyrimidines (C/T), B represents G/T/C, and M represents A/C, enrichment e value = 2.6*10–109).
source: Based on all the sequences enriched in the ChIP analysis under glucose and propionate conditions, the conserved binding motif for Rv0158 was found to be YGGCGGBGMCGGCGG (where Y represents pyrimidines (C/T), B represents G/T/C, and M represents A/C, enrichment e value = 2.6*10–109; Figure 11D).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif analysis data shown in Figure 11D.

claim: The enriched motif was present close to the binding motifs of other transcription factors involved in regulating MCC (e.g. PrpR, GlnR, PhoP, and RamB).
source: Interestingly, the enriched motif was present close to the binding motifs of other transcription factors involved in regulating MCC (e.g. PrpR, GlnR, PhoP, and RamB; Supplementary file 6), suggesting overlapping or competing mechanisms to regulate propionate metabolism in Mtb.
evidence: The claim is supported by motif analysis data shown in Supplementary file 6.

claim: rv0158 KO showed greater killing by 10–100-fold to H2O2, CHP, menadione, and ≈ four fold to the nitric-oxide donor DETA-NO than WT Mtb and rv0158 Comp.
source: We found that rv0158 KO showed greater killing by 10–100-fold to H2O2, CHP, menadione, and ≈ four fold to the nitric-oxide donor DETA-NO than WT Mtb and rv0158 Comp (Figure 12A).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 12A.

claim: The sensitivity of rv0158 KO towards H2O2 stress was alleviated when glucose was substituted with fatty acids (0.03% acetate or 0.3% propionate or 0.02% cholesterol) as C source.
source: Interestingly, the sensitivity of rv0158 KO towards H2O2 stress was alleviated when glucose was substituted with fatty acids (0.03% acetate or 0.3% propionate or 0.02% cholesterol) as C source (Figure 12—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 12—figure supplement 1.

claim: The minimal inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of anti-TB drugs in the case of rv0158 KO showed a modest decrease by two fold as compared to WT Mtb and rv0158 Comp.
source: The minimal inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of anti-TB drugs in the case of rv0158 KO showed a modest decrease by two fold as compared to WT Mtb and rv0158 Comp (Table 3, Figure 12—figure supplement 2b–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by MIC data shown in Table 3 and Figure 12—figure supplement 2b–d.

claim: Treatment with 1 X MIC of isoniazid (MIC = 0.06 μg/mL), moxifloxacin (MIC = 0.125 μg/mL), and bedaquiline (MIC = 0.03 μg/mL) for 5 days decreased the survival of rv0158 KO by >10-fold relative to WT Mtb.
source: Treatment with 1 X MIC of isoniazid (MIC = 0.06 μg/mL), moxifloxacin (MIC = 0.125 μg/mL), and bedaquiline (MIC = 0.03 μg/mL) for 5 days decreased the survival of rv0158 KO by >10-fold relative to WT Mtb (Figure 12B).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 12B.

claim: A greater proportion of rv0158 KO cells were detected in an EMSH-oxidized state at 48 hr post-infection than WT Mtb and rv0158 Comp.
source: Interestingly, we detected a greater proportion of rv0158 KO cells in an EMSH-oxidized state at 48 hr post-infection (p.i.) than WT Mtb and rv0158 Comp (Figure 12C).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 12C.

claim: The increased oxidative shift in the EMSH of rv0158 KO correlated with bacteriostasis at 2 days p.i. and ≈50% killing at 4 days p.i.
source: The increased oxidative shift in the EMSH of rv0158 KO correlated with bacteriostasis at 2 days p.i. and ≈50% killing at 4 days p.i. (Figure 12D).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 12D.

claim: At 4- and 8 weeks post-infection, the bacterial burden in the lungs of mice infected with rv0158 KO was ≈2 and ≈10-fold lower than those infected with WT Mtb, respectively.
source: At 4- and 8 weeks post-infection, the bacterial burden in the lungs of mice infected with rv0158 KO was ≈2 and ≈10-fold lower than those infected with WT Mtb, respectively (Figure 12F).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU data from mouse infection shown in Figure 12F.

claim: At 4- and 8 weeks post-infection, bacterial numbers in the spleen decreased by about 3-fold and 28-fold, respectively.
source: Similarly, at 4- and 8 weeks post-infection, bacterial numbers in the spleen decreased by about 3-fold and 28-fold, respectively (Figure 12G).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU data from mouse infection shown in Figure 12G.

claim: The phenotype exhibited by rv0158 KO was mostly restored in mice infected with the complemented strain.
source: The phenotype exhibited by rv0158 KO was mostly restored in mice infected with the complemented strain (Figure 12F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU data from mouse infection shown in Figure 12F and G.

claim: rv0158 is required for the persistence of Mtb.
source: The data indicate that rv0158 is required for the persistence of Mtb.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the mouse infection data.
